A Digital Museum of Dance & History

From Harlem ballrooms to Cold War stages, follow the dancers who found room to improvise in a world shaped by war, politics, and social rules.

Explore the timeline Open the magazine

✦ The exhibition question

How has dance reflected
and influenced history?

Dance reflects who can gather, what music can play, and whose bodies are welcome in public. It also changes what people can do together. A dance floor can sustain a community, give young people room to defy authority, or let audiences meet artists their governments call rivals.

The timeline

A century in steps

Choose an era, then play or step through a short movement study to see how its dance uses weight, timing, or space.

1920s
–30s

Harlem, New York · 1920s–30s

Lindy Hop takes shape

Black dancers in Harlem developed Lindy Hop in conversation with jazz musicians and with one another. The Savoy Ballroom gave dancers room to improvise. As the form spread, a practice rooted in Black social life became part of American popular culture.

Hancock, 2013

1939
–45

Hamburg, Germany · 1939–45

Swing under surveillance

Young swing enthusiasts gathered around jazz, dancing, and styles that marked their distance from Nazi youth culture. Authorities cracked down. Their gatherings reveal how even leisure could become a political matter under dictatorship.

Kater, 2003

1943

Washington, D.C. · April 1943

A night at the Elks Club

Esther Bubley photographed people dancing the jitterbug during wartime mobilization. In the photograph, two dancers look down at their feet while several other couples fill the room. Their attention to the steps makes an ordinary night out part of the historical record.

Bubley, 1943

1959
–62

United States and Soviet Union · 1959–62

Ballet crosses the Cold War divide

The Bolshoi Ballet toured the United States in 1959. New York City Ballet performed in the Soviet Union in 1962. Each tour put a rival country’s artists before audiences who could make up their own minds about the work.

Searcy, 2020

20th
c.

United States · Late 20th century

What does it mean to bring swing back?

A new wave of dancers embraced Lindy Hop. Studying Chicago dance communities, sociologist Black Hawk Hancock examined how revivals can circulate a Black cultural form while obscuring its origins and the inequalities around it.

Hancock, 2013

The magazine

Dance in print

Turn the pages, then open the archive to examine the 1947 cover or read the full February 1962 issue.

1947–1948 · Barn dance radio

Song and Picture Barn Dance Magazine

This magazine brought postwar American country music and rural radio culture into print. It profiled radio barn dance performers and country-western musicians, pairing song lyrics with photographs. Traditional square dance calls were part of the barn dance culture those broadcasts shared with listeners.

The 1947 cover features country singer Elton Britt. It gives a face to a performer listeners might have known only by voice.

Open Smithsonian record Enlarge the cover

The Smithsonian provides a cover scan for this issue.

1948–1985 · Square and round dancing

Sets in Order

The magazine documented the American square and round dance revival. It published choreography and step-by-step guidance for callers, the people who prompt dancers through a sequence. Club news, meeting notices, and event listings connected readers to the social life around the dances.

The February 1962 cover shows a couple in a promenade and points readers to a story about square dance organization. The two details capture the magazine’s interest in both the steps and the clubs that brought people together.

Dance & history

Dance in a time of conflict

Three cases show what dancing could mean under dictatorship, during wartime, and across a geopolitical divide.

Hamburg
1939–45

Swing Youth under Nazi rule

Young people in Hamburg gathered to listen and dance to swing. Their attachment to American and British jazz and their distinctive style ran against Nazi demands for cultural and social conformity. Jazz had strong Black American roots, and Jewish musicians also played important roles in European jazz. Nazi racial ideology made the music a target, even though enforcement and restrictions varied.

Authorities monitored gatherings, made arrests, and sent some young people to camps. Individual motives varied, from pleasure and friendship to open defiance. The crackdown shows how an authoritarian state could turn a musical preference into evidence of disloyalty.

Kater, 2003

Watch: Swing Kids in Hamburg

In this PBS interview, scholar Les Back discusses underground jazz in wartime Germany. The interview was recorded after the war.

Open the interview at PBS

United States
1940s

Wartime social dancing

Dance offered occasions for sociability amid wartime work, travel, and uncertainty. Bubley’s Washington photograph records an Elks Club dance. Other wartime photographs show jitterbugging among troops preparing to depart and formal social dances at officers’ clubs. These settings had different purposes, from a night out to organized recreation.

Photographs also record dancing among Japanese Americans imprisoned by the U.S. government. Dancing there could sustain social life under confinement. The photographs establish that dancing took place in these settings. A caption alone cannot tell us how participants felt, who was excluded, or whether the photographer staged a scene.

Bubley, 1943 Hammerich, 2022

Watch: Jitterbug and jive in 1943

British Pathé filmed dancers at the Hammersmith Palais in London. Watch the partners’ footwork and how people take up the dance together.

Open British Pathé’s 1943 newsreel

U.S. and U.S.S.R.
1959–62

Ballet and Cold War diplomacy

The Bolshoi Ballet’s 1959 U.S. tour and New York City Ballet’s 1962 Soviet tour were part of a bilateral cultural exchange. Officials used performances to project prestige and create moments of goodwill. The New York City Ballet tour unfolded during the Cuban Missile Crisis, when the stakes of official relations were especially visible.

Dance historian Anne Searcy shows that spectators interpreted visiting companies through local artistic expectations. The tours created contact even while political conflict continued. Their significance lies partly in what dancers and spectators made of those encounters for themselves.

Searcy, 2020

Watch: The Bolshoi Ballet opens in 1959

This WSB-TV newsfilm documents the Bolshoi’s 1959 American visit, one of the exchanges described above.

Then vs. Now

What travels with a dance?

Compare how dances circulate and how people learn to credit the communities that created them.

Then

The ballroom and the printed page

Dancers could learn steps by watching others in the room. Records carried swing across borders. In the United States, magazines such as Sets in Order gave callers written instructions they could take from one dance floor to another.

Hancock, 2013 Kater, 2003 Explore the magazine

Now

The workshop and the screen

A dancer can encounter a step at a local social, a workshop, or in a short video. Try comparing a tutorial with a social-dance recording. What can each show about how dancers respond to partners and musicians?

Then

Harlem’s Black innovators

Lindy Hop spread from Black dance communities. Its later popularity invites us to ask whose invention is remembered when a dance becomes part of a national story.

Hancock, 2013

Now

Credit as part of learning

Look at how a class description, event program, or clip names the dance’s origins. Who is named as an innovator, who is invited to teach, and what history can learners find?

Hancock, 2013

Research

Sources from the reading room

Three scholarly books frame the exhibit. An archival photograph and a university account of archival research ground the wartime case. Two magazine covers show how American publishers documented barn dance radio and organized square dancing.

Read the catalog records alongside the images. Look at which performers, dances, and groups each publication chose to feature.

PFA 222 Creative Response

Intent statement

When we started The World in Motion, I wanted to understand how dance has reflected and influenced history. I usually think of dance as something people do for fun or to express themselves. What interested me was how much you can learn by asking where people danced, who could join them, and what was happening around them.

One example that stood out to me was the Swing Youth in Nazi Germany. Some young people wanted to listen to jazz and dance with their friends. The authorities saw that as a threat. In the United States during World War II, social dancing gave some people a chance to spend time together during a stressful period. Later, Cold War ballet tours gave audiences a chance to see artists from a country their government treated as a rival.

We made a digital museum so people could explore the examples at their own pace. The timeline puts the events in order. In the magazine, visitors can turn from a 1947 cover of Song and Picture Barn Dance Magazine to a 1962 cover of Sets in Order. I liked seeing how one magazine introduced readers to radio performers, while the other helped dancers and callers share steps and stay connected. Then vs. Now asks how people share dances and give credit to the communities that created them. We gave the website an aged paper look because we wanted it to feel like a museum guide you could flip through.

I hope visitors leave thinking about what a dance can tell them about the people who do it. Getting together and moving to music can mean something different depending on the place, the people, and the rules. We added a museum quiz at the end so classmates can revisit the examples and see what they remember.
